content: Xanthines, such as theophylline, have historically been used as bronchodilators in the treatment of asthma, and they may also possess anti-inflammatory properties. However, their role in the long-term management of asthma in children requires reevaluation. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy of xanthines in the maintenance treatment of pediatric asthma. Randomized controlled trials lasting at least four weeks were included, comparing xanthines with placebo, short-acting beta-agonists (SABA), inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), sodium cromoglycate (SCG), ketotifen (KET), or leukotriene receptor antagonists in children aged 18 months to 18 years with chronic asthma. The primary outcome was the percentage of symptom-free days. A total of 36 studies involving 2838 participants were included in the analysis. 1. Xanthine versus Placebo (18 studies): Xanthines were associated with a higher proportion of symptom-free days compared to placebo (7.97% improvement, 95% CI 3.41 to 12.53). Use of rescue medication was reduced with xanthines. Lung function, as measured by FEV1 and PEF, was better with xanthines. There were no significant differences in symptom scores or hospitalizations. Xanthines were linked to non-specific side effects, but data on behavioral outcomes were inconclusive. 2. Xanthine versus ICS (4 studies): Exacerbations were less frequent with ICS compared to xanthines. No significant differences in lung function were observed between the two treatments. Individual studies showed better symptom control with ICS, while one study reported a growth rate advantage with xanthines. Xanthines were associated with more frequent headaches and nausea, but no differences in study withdrawal rates or tremor were noted. 3. Xanthine versus Regular SABA (10 studies): No significant differences were found in symptoms, rescue medication use, or spirometry outcomes. Some studies reported improved PEF with beta-agonists. Beta-agonists were associated with fewer hospitalizations and headaches, while xanthines caused less tremor. 4. Xanthine versus SCG (6 studies): No significant differences were observed in symptoms, exacerbations, or rescue medication use. Sodium cromoglycate was associated with fewer gastrointestinal side effects compared to xanthines. 5. Xanthine versus Ketotifen (1 study): No statistical comparisons were reported between xanthines and ketotifen. 6. Xanthine + ICS versus Placebo + ICS (3 studies): Results were inconsistent due to clinical and methodological differences, preventing aggregation of data. 7. Xanthine + ICS versus ICS + Leukotriene Antagonist (1 study): A single small study did not measure symptom outcomes, and differences in end-of-treatment values were not statistically significant. Conclusions: Xanthines can reduce symptoms and the need for rescue medication in children with mild to moderate asthma when used as a first-line preventative treatment. However, they are less effective than ICS in preventing exacerbations. Xanthines demonstrated similar efficacy to regular SABA and SCG as single preventative agents. Adverse effects (AEs) were more frequent overall with xanthines, but no specific AE, including behavioral or attention-related effects, occurred more frequently than with placebo. There is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about the effectiveness of xanthines as an add-on therapy to ICS, and no pediatric studies have compared xanthines with other alternatives in this role. Xanthines may be considered as a first-line preventative therapy only when ICS are unavailable. They could potentially serve as add-on therapy in severe asthma not controlled by ICS, but further research is needed to evaluate their risk-benefit profile compared to other agents. Pre-trial exposure to xanthines may have influenced tolerance and blinding in the included studies.
